title: Tissues
note: The body is built from four tissue types: epithelial, connective, muscle, and nervous. Epithelia are named by layers (simple, stratified) plus the shape of the surface cells (squamous, cuboidal, columnar). Connective tissues are defined by their extracellular matrix.

read.title: Reading an epithelium's name
text: An epithelium's name is a short description of what it looks like, and the look tells you what it does. The first word counts layers. Simple means one layer, which is ideal where things must cross quickly, as in the air sacs of the lungs. Stratified means many layers, which is ideal where a surface takes wear, as in the skin and the lining of the mouth.

The second word names the shape of the cells at the free surface. Squamous cells are flat, cuboidal cells are about as tall as wide, and columnar cells are taller than wide. Thicker cells have room for the machinery of secretion and absorption, so cuboidal and columnar cells line kidney tubules, gland ducts, and much of the gut.

Two names break the pattern. Pseudostratified epithelium is really a single layer whose nuclei sit at different heights, and in the airways it carries cilia that sweep mucus upward. Transitional epithelium lines the urinary bladder and can flatten as the bladder stretches.

Connective tissues are named differently. They are defined mainly by their extracellular matrix: the fibers and ground substance their cells secrete. Collagen fibers resist pulling, elastic fibers stretch and recoil, and the matrix of bone is hardened with mineral.

q.q: Why is simple squamous epithelium found in the lung's air sacs?
o: A single flat layer lets gases cross quickly

q.q: What mainly defines a connective tissue?
o: The shape of its surface cells
